---
title: "Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons"
---

## Introduction {#sec-qba-intro}

When a health technology assessment (HTA) committee, for example a NICE appraisal panel or an FDA
advisory committee, must decide whether to reimburse a new treatment against an established comparator,
the pivotal evidence is frequently an indirect comparison rather than a head-to-head trial. The
committee's sharpest question is seldom "what is the point estimate?" but "how confident are you that the
estimate survives a covariate you were never able to adjust for?" This chapter develops the mathematics of
answering that question honestly, so that a reimbursement dossier can report not merely an effect but a
defensible statement about how fragile that effect is.

Every method in this book up to now has removed bias by *measuring* the variable that causes it. The
anchored Bucher comparison (@thm-bucher-unbiased) is exact when every effect modifier is shared and
common; matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18) reweights the individual patient data (IPD)
until the imbalanced effect modifiers are balanced; simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and
multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20) model the same covariates inside an outcome regression.
All of them adjust for a covariate by using it. What none of them can do is adjust for a covariate that
was never measured, or, in the most common and most dangerous case for an unanchored indirect comparison,
one that the comparator publication never reported.

The distinction is worth a table, because it says precisely where this chapter begins. Each earlier method
neutralizes a covariate only by having access to it in some form; QBA is what remains when even that access
is gone.

| Method | How it removes the covariate's bias | What it needs the covariate to be |
|---|---|---|
| Bucher (Chapter 14) | cancels it through a common comparator arm | shared and balanced across trials |
| MAIC (Chapter 18) | reweights the IPD until it is balanced | measured in the IPD, summarized by the comparator |
| STC (Chapter 19) | enters it in an outcome regression | measured in the IPD, summarized by the comparator |
| ML-NMR (Chapter 20) | integrates the outcome model over it | measured in the IPD, summarized by the comparator |
| QBA (this chapter) | quantifies what it *could* be doing | neither measured nor reported |

The threat is sharpest in the unanchored setting. Chapter 17 showed that an unanchored
population-adjusted indirect comparison (PAIC) is consistent only under conditional constancy of
*absolute* effects and balance of every imbalanced *prognostic* variable, not merely the effect
modifiers (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency, @def-conditional-constancy-absolute), and Chapter 12 showed
that the shared-effect-modifier assumption is by itself insufficient to identify the target-population
contrast (@thm-sema-insufficient). The single covariate that escapes the analysis, an unmeasured effect
modifier (@def-effect-modifier) whose distribution differs between the two trial populations, is residual
bias that no reweighting and no outcome model can touch, because the quantity it depends on, the
covariate's distribution in the comparator population, is simply unknown. The honest response is not to
pretend the bias is zero but to *quantify* it: to ask how large the unmeasured mechanism would have to be
to matter, and to report the answer alongside the point estimate. This is **quantitative bias analysis**
(QBA), the subject of this chapter.

::: {.remark}
**Prognostic variable versus effect modifier, in one line.** Two kinds of covariate recur throughout the
book, and the difference decides which comparisons they threaten. A **prognostic variable** shifts a
patient's outcome risk regardless of which treatment they take; an **effect modifier** changes the *size of
the treatment effect* itself, so the benefit of $B$ over $A$ differs across its levels (@def-effect-modifier).
An *anchored* comparison, which subtracts a within-trial contrast, is undisturbed by a purely prognostic
variable and needs only its effect modifiers balanced; an *unanchored* comparison has no such protection
and needs balance of *every* imbalanced prognostic variable as well (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency).
That is why the unreported covariate is the sharpest threat exactly in the unanchored setting, and why the
running example below places its unreported covariate there. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

QBA originates in epidemiology, where the same three threats to validity recur in every observational
study: uncontrolled confounding, selection of the study sample on exposure and outcome, and
mismeasurement of variables. The canonical reference is the monograph of @lash2021qba, whose deterministic
and probabilistic machinery we adapt. We develop four instruments, in increasing sophistication. First,
the **E-value** of @vanderweele2017evalue: a single number, derived from the point estimate alone, giving
the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding or effect modification, on the risk-ratio scale, that
could explain the observed effect away. We give its full derivation, resting on a sharp bound for the
confounding bias factor that we prove from scratch. Second, an **indirect-comparison-specific E-value**
that exploits a structural feature unique to the unanchored ITC: the unmeasured covariate is observed in
the analyst's own IPD, so half of the sensitivity problem is estimable rather than assumed, and the
resulting E-value is sharper and can certify a result as provably robust. Third, the **NORTA**
(normal-to-anything) construction, which imputes the unreported joint distribution of the comparator's
covariates by gluing the reported margins to a dependence structure borrowed from the IPD through a
Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula, @thm-inverse-cdf); we prove that the construction reproduces the
margins exactly and induces precisely the intended copula. Fourth, the **tipping-point** analysis and its
probabilistic upgrade, which locate the assumed value of the unreported covariate at which the conclusion
reverses and place a prior distribution over that value to propagate the uncertainty honestly.

This material is new to the formal theory of indirect comparison; it is not in the proof catalogue, and
it has no machine-checked counterpart in the companion Coq development. We therefore build it from first
principles, proving every bound in full and grounding each tool in a fully worked, hand-checkable example
at the end of the chapter.

Throughout, $g$ is the link function on whose scale effects are reported and modeled, and $g^{-1}$ its
inverse; for binary and count outcomes the analysis scale is the log odds ratio or log rate ratio, so
the effects of interest live on the risk-ratio scale where the E-value is defined. We write $\mathrm{RR}$,
$\mathrm{OR}$, $\mathrm{HR}$ for risk, odds, and hazard ratios as in [Notation](/notation.qmd). The
symbol $U$ denotes the *unmeasured* (in the confounding sense) or *unreported* (in the ITC sense)
covariate, distinguished from the measured covariate vector $\mathbf{x}$; $\mathbf{b}$ denotes a vector
of **bias parameters**; and we reserve the plain italic $E$ for the E-value, distinct from the
expectation operator $\mathbb{E}[\cdot]$.

This chapter builds five instruments. They are not competitors but a toolkit: some answer *how robust is
the estimate?*, one answers *what value would overturn it?*, one answers *how do I propagate my uncertainty
about that value?*, and one is the machinery that builds the comparator population the others need. Keep
the following map in view.

| Instrument | Question it answers | Main input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| E-value (@sec-qba-evalue) | how strong must unmeasured confounding be to explain the estimate away? | the point estimate on the risk-ratio scale | one number $E$ |
| ITC E-value (@sec-qba-itc-evalue) | the same, using the outcome association measured in the IPD | point estimate plus $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ from the IPD | $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}$, possibly $+\infty$ |
| NORTA (@sec-qba-norta) | how do I build a comparator population to recompute the effect? | reported margins plus IPD dependence | a simulated covariate population |
| Tipping point (@sec-qba-tipping) | what comparator value flips the conclusion? | a sensitivity curve and a threshold | a value $m^{\dagger}$ in covariate units |
| Probabilistic bias analysis (@sec-qba-probabilistic) | how does uncertainty about that value propagate? | a prior on the bias parameter plus the sampling error | systematic and total intervals |

We anchor all five to one concrete comparison, introduced now and computed in full in @sec-qba-example.

::: {#exm-qba-running}
## A running example: an unanchored COPD comparison
A manufacturer seeks reimbursement for a new inhaled therapy $B$ for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD). Only a single-arm trial of $B$ is available, with full individual patient data (IPD); the
established comparator $A$ has only a published summary. The outcome is a *severe exacerbation within 12
months*, a bad event, so a risk ratio below $1$ favors $B$. Two baseline covariates matter. The first,
$x_R$, is age (standardized), which the $A$ publication reports as a mean and standard deviation. The
second, $u$, is baseline lung function $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ (forced expiratory volume in one second, in liters;
higher is healthier, so it lowers exacerbation risk): the $A$ publication does *not* report it at all. An
unanchored analysis that plugs the IPD value of $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ into the comparator population returns an
adjusted risk ratio of about $\mathrm{RR}=0.50$ ($95\%$ confidence interval $0.30$ to $0.81$), so $B$ appears
to roughly halve the exacerbation risk. The committee's question is the subject of this chapter: *how much
of that apparent benefit could be an artifact of the unreported* $\mathrm{FEV}_1$?

We carry this trial through every instrument below, previewing each result where the instrument is defined
and computing all of it by hand in @sec-qba-example. The model fitted to the IPD, with a log link on the
risk, is $\log P(Y=1\mid x_R,u)=\beta_0+\beta_R x_R+\beta_U u$ with $\beta_0=-1.0$, $\beta_R=0.4$ (older
age raises risk), and $\beta_U=-0.5$ (higher $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ lowers risk); the comparator reports age mean
$m_R=1.0$, standard deviation $\sigma_R=0.5$, and its own event risk $\mu_0=0.47$, and in the IPD the
covariate $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ has mean $\bar{x}_U=2.0$ and standard deviation $\sigma_U=1.0$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The framework of bias analysis {#sec-qba-framework}

Bias analysis begins by writing down, explicitly, the mechanism that links what we observe to what is
true. An estimate is *valid* when the estimator converges to the estimand; it is *biased* by a systematic
error when a structural feature of the data, distinct from sampling variability, drives a wedge between
the two. Quantitative bias analysis makes that wedge a function of named, interpretable parameters and
then explores it.

A natural first reaction to a worrying covariate is to fit a richer model that includes it. The reason
that does not work here is worth stating plainly: in an unanchored indirect comparison the covariate is
*unreported by the comparator*, so there is no column for it in the comparator data and no likelihood can
condition on it. Bayesian model expansion is the right tool when you hold the data and merely distrust a
functional form; quantitative bias analysis is the right tool when the data themselves are missing and the
best you can do is ask how bad the omission could be. QBA does not recover the missing information; it
bounds the damage.

::: {#def-quantitative-bias-analysis}
## Quantitative bias analysis
Let $\theta$ be a target estimand and $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}$ an estimator that is consistent for a
biased surrogate $\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}=\theta\cdot B(\mathbf{b})$ (multiplicative scale) or
$\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}=\theta + B(\mathbf{b})$ (additive scale), where the **bias function** $B$ depends
on a vector of **bias parameters** $\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{B}$ that index the unverified structural
assumptions (the strength and imbalance of an unmeasured confounder, the selection probabilities of each
cell, the sensitivity and specificity of a mismeasured variable, or the comparator distribution of an
unreported covariate). A **quantitative bias analysis** is the map
$$
\mathbf{b}\;\longmapsto\;\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b})
\;=\;h\big(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}},\mathbf{b}\big),
$$ {#eq-qba-correction}
where the **correction** $h$ inverts the bias model, returning the value of the target consistent with
the observed estimate under the assumed $\mathbf{b}$. The analysis is **deterministic** when $\mathbf{b}$
ranges over a fixed grid or a single value, and **probabilistic** when $\mathbf{b}$ carries a prior
distribution $\pi$ that is propagated to a distribution over $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}$. The three
classical threats, **uncontrolled confounding**, **selection bias**, and **misclassification**, are the
corners of the *bias triangle* and each supplies its own $B$ and $h$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation.** Read @def-quantitative-bias-analysis as a recipe with three moves: (i) *name* the
unverified quantities as a parameter vector $\mathbf{b}$ (how imbalanced the missing covariate is, how
strongly it acts, and so on); (ii) *write* the bias as an explicit function $B(\mathbf{b})$ of them; (iii)
*invert* it to see what the honest estimate would have been. On the multiplicative scale the correction
divides: $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}/B(\mathbf{b})$, as in the risk-ratio
confounding factor below. On the additive scale it subtracts: for a risk difference distorted by a
selection or misclassification shift $B(\mathbf{b})$, the corrected estimate is
$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{obs}}-B(\mathbf{b})$. The three corners of the bias triangle just supply three
different shapes of $B$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### A practical workflow {#sec-qba-workflow}

Before the derivations, here is the applied procedure the rest of the chapter makes precise, written as a
health researcher would run it for an unanchored indirect comparison.

1. **Identify the threat.** Name the covariate that is imbalanced and unreported by the comparator, and
decide whether it is prognostic, an effect modifier, or both.
2. **Estimate what you can.** From the IPD, read off the covariate's association with the outcome,
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)$ on a ratio scale, and its own IPD distribution.
3. **Screen with an E-value.** Compute the E-value and, using $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, the sharper
indirect-comparison E-value (@sec-qba-itc-evalue). If the latter is $+\infty$, stop: the result is certified
robust to this covariate.
4. **Choose plausible comparator values.** Fix a range or a prior for the covariate's comparator marginal
from external evidence (registries, related trials, elicitation); this is a sensitivity assumption, not new
data.
5. **Build the comparator population.** If dependence with the reported covariates matters, use NORTA
(@sec-qba-norta) to glue your assumed marginal to a dependence structure borrowed from the IPD; otherwise
the marginal alone suffices.
6. **Compute the sensitivity curve and its tipping point.** Marginalize the IPD outcome model over each
assumed value to get $\Delta(m)$, and locate the value $m^{\dagger}$ at which the conclusion reverses
(@sec-qba-tipping).
7. **Propagate the uncertainty.** Place a prior on the comparator marginal and report the systematic and
total intervals and the probability of benefit (@sec-qba-probabilistic).
8. **Report honestly.** State the E-value, the tipping point in the covariate's own units, and whether a
believable comparator value would overturn the conclusion.

The sections below justify each step; the running example runs all eight. A handful of risk-ratio labels
recur across those steps, so the following dictionary fixes them once.

| Symbol | How to read it |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}$, $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ | the confounded thing the data show, before removing bias (used interchangeably) |
| $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}$, $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{true}}$ | the de-biased target you would see with the confounder controlled (likewise interchangeable) |
| $B(\mathbf{b})$ | the general bias *function* of @def-quantitative-bias-analysis |
| $B$ (no argument) | the specific confounding bias *factor* of @lem-qba-confounding-factor, one instance of $B(\mathbf{b})$ |
| $\mathrm{RR}_{XY}$ | the risk ratio of $Y$ across levels of $X$ (so $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$, $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ read off the roles $E$ = exposure, $U$ = unmeasured covariate, $D$ = disease) |
| $E$ (italic), $\mathbb{E}$ | the E-value @eq-qba-evalue and the expectation operator: never the exposure, which we write $A$ |

The simplest instance, and the one that motivates the E-value, is a single binary unmeasured confounder
acting on a risk ratio. We derive its correction now, both because it is the prototype of
@eq-qba-correction and because the E-value is exactly the question "how large must $\mathbf{b}$ be?" asked
of this model.

::: {#lem-qba-confounding-factor}
## Confounding bias factor for a binary confounder
Consider a binary exposure (treatment) $A\in\{0,1\}$, a binary outcome $D$, and a binary unmeasured
confounder $U\in\{0,1\}$ with prevalence $p_1=P(U=1\mid A=1)$ among the exposed and $p_0=P(U=1\mid A=0)$
among the unexposed. Suppose $U$ is the only confounder, so that within strata of $U$ the exposure is
unconfounded, and suppose $U$ acts on the outcome with a constant risk ratio
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=P(D=1\mid U=1,A=a)/P(D=1\mid U=0,A=a)$ that does not depend on $a$. Then the crude
(confounded) risk ratio and the $U$-adjusted risk ratio differ by the multiplicative **bias factor**
$$
B \;=\; \frac{p_1\,(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)+1}{p_0\,(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)+1},
\qquad
\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}=\frac{\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}}{B}.
$$ {#eq-qba-bias-factor}
In particular $B=1$ when $p_1=p_0$ (the confounder is balanced) or $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1$ (the confounder
is inert).
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $r_a=P(D=1\mid A=a)$ for the marginal risk in arm $a$ and $q_a(u)=P(D=1\mid A=a,U=u)$ for the
stratum risks. The lemma's constant-risk-ratio hypothesis says exactly that the within-arm outcome risk
ratio across $U$ is $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, that is $q_a(1)/q_a(0)=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, so
$q_a(1)=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\,q_a(0)$. By the law of total probability,
$r_a=q_a(0)\,(1-p_a)+q_a(1)\,p_a=q_a(0)\big[(1-p_a)+p_a\,\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\big]=q_a(0)\big[1+p_a(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)\big]$.
The crude risk ratio is therefore
$$
\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}=\frac{r_1}{r_0}
=\frac{q_1(0)}{q_0(0)}\cdot\frac{1+p_1(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{1+p_0(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}.
$$
Because $U$ is the only confounder, the ratio $q_1(0)/q_0(0)$ of the stratum-$U{=}0$ risks is the
unconfounded, $U$-adjusted risk ratio $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}$ (the within-stratum exposure effect,
assumed constant across $U$). The remaining factor is exactly $B$ in @eq-qba-bias-factor, so
$\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{crude}}=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{adj}}\cdot B$, which rearranges to the stated
correction. Setting $p_1=p_0$ makes numerator and denominator equal, $B=1$; setting $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1$
makes both equal $1$, again $B=1$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the bias factor says.** In words, the crude estimate you see equals the true effect times a factor
that measures how differently the confounder is spread across the two arms. That factor is a product of two
intuitions the formula makes exact: a confounder equally common in both arms ($p_1=p_0$) cannot bias
anything, and a confounder unrelated to the outcome ($\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1$) cannot either. Bias needs *both*
an imbalance and an outcome link, which is exactly why an unreported covariate is dangerous only when it is
both differently distributed across the trials and prognostic. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The deterministic correction needs three numbers you rarely have.** Formula @eq-qba-bias-factor is the
correction $h$ of @def-quantitative-bias-analysis with bias parameters
$\mathbf{b}=(p_1,p_0,\mathrm{RR}_{UD})$. It is honest but demanding: it presumes the analyst can name the
prevalence of the unmeasured confounder in each arm and its outcome association. Selection bias and
misclassification have analogous corrections (the selection odds ratio divides out of the crude odds
ratio; the classification correction inverts the sensitivity-specificity map cell by cell), each with its
own $\mathbf{b}$; see @lash2021qba. The E-value of the next section sidesteps the need to specify
$\mathbf{b}$ by turning the question around. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The other two corners: selection and misclassification {#sec-qba-other-corners}

The bias triangle has three vertices, and the rest of this chapter develops only the confounding vertex,
because it is the one that maps directly onto the unreported effect modifier of an unanchored comparison.
For completeness we record the other two corrections, both standard and both taken from @lash2021qba rather
than re-derived here, so the reader can see the common shape: each names bias parameters, writes a $B$, and
inverts it.

**Selection bias.** When inclusion in the analysis depends on both exposure and outcome, let $s_{ad}$ be
the probability that a subject with exposure $a\in\{0,1\}$ and outcome $d\in\{0,1\}$ enters the sample. The
observed (selected-sample) odds ratio and the target-population odds ratio differ by the multiplicative
selection bias factor
$$
B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\frac{s_{11}\,s_{00}}{s_{10}\,s_{01}},
\qquad
\mathrm{OR}_{\mathrm{adj}}=\frac{\mathrm{OR}_{\mathrm{obs}}}{B_{\mathrm{sel}}},
$$ {#eq-qba-selection-factor}
so selection is harmless exactly when the four selection probabilities factor into an exposure term times
an outcome term (no exposure-by-outcome interaction in who gets in).

**Misclassification.** When a binary exposure is measured with sensitivity $\mathrm{Se}=P(A^{*}=1\mid A=1)$
and specificity $\mathrm{Sp}=P(A^{*}=0\mid A=0)$, where $A^{*}$ is the recorded and $A$ the true exposure,
the true exposed count $N_1$ in a stratum of size $n$ with observed exposed count $N_1^{*}$ is recovered by
inverting the classification map,
$$
N_1=\frac{N_1^{*}-(1-\mathrm{Sp})\,n}{\mathrm{Se}+\mathrm{Sp}-1},
$$ {#eq-qba-misclass-correction}
valid whenever $\mathrm{Se}+\mathrm{Sp}>1$ (the measurement is better than a coin flip); one applies it
within outcome strata and recomputes the effect from the corrected counts. Both corrections have
probabilistic upgrades, priors on $(s_{ad})$ or on $(\mathrm{Se},\mathrm{Sp})$, exactly as in
@sec-qba-probabilistic. In an indirect comparison the confounding corner dominates, so from here on *bias*
means residual imbalance in an unreported covariate unless stated otherwise.

## The E-value {#sec-qba-evalue}

The E-value asks not "what is the bias, given $\mathbf{b}$?" but "how strong must $\mathbf{b}$ be to
overturn the conclusion?" To answer it we need a bound that holds for *any* unmeasured confounder, not
just a binary one with a constant association, in terms of two scalar sensitivity parameters. The bound
of @vanderweele2017evalue, building on the bias-factor analysis of Ding and VanderWeele, is sharp, and we
prove it in full.

Fix a binary exposure $A$ and binary outcome $D$, with an unmeasured confounder $U$ taking values in a
finite set $\mathcal{U}$. Write $f_a(u)=P(U=u\mid A=a)$ for the confounder distribution in arm $a$ and
$p_a(u)=P(D=1\mid A=a,U=u)$ for the stratum risks. Define the two **sensitivity parameters**
$$
\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\;=\;\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\frac{f_1(u)}{f_0(u)},
\qquad
\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\;=\;\frac{\max_{u}p_0(u)}{\min_{u}p_0(u)},
$$ {#eq-qba-sensitivity-params}
both at least $1$. A word on the subscripts, which follow the E-value literature and are unrelated to the
italic E-value $E$ of @eq-qba-evalue or to the expectation $\mathbb{E}$: in $\mathrm{RR}_{XY}$ the pair
$XY$ reads "the risk ratio of $Y$ across levels of $X$", with $E$ naming the exposure role (the treatment
variable we write $A$), $U$ the unmeasured covariate, and $D$ the disease outcome. So $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$
measures how exposure shifts the confounder distribution and $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ how the confounder shifts
outcome risk. In words, $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$ is the largest factor by which any confounder level is
over-represented in the exposed relative to the unexposed arm, and $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ is the widest spread
of outcome risk across confounder levels within the unexposed arm.

::: {.remark}
**A number to hold onto.** Suppose a biomarker is twice as common in the exposed arm as in the unexposed
arm, $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=2$, and carries a threefold spread in outcome risk, $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=3$. The bound
below says the most these two facts can bias a risk ratio is
$\mathrm{BF}_U=\dfrac{2\times 3}{2+3-1}=\dfrac{6}{4}=1.5$: no configuration of that confounder can inflate
an observed risk ratio by more than a factor of $1.5$. The next lemma proves this formula and, crucially,
that $1.5$ is *attained*, not merely an over-cautious ceiling. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#lem-qba-sharp-bound}
## Sharp bound on the confounding bias factor
With the notation above, suppose $U$ carries all the confounding, so that within strata of $U$ the
exposure is unconfounded. Then the confounding bias factor $B$ relating the observed risk ratio to the
$U$-adjusted (causal) risk ratio standardized to the exposed (that is, averaging the stratum risks over the
exposed arm's confounder distribution) satisfies
$$
B\;\le\;\mathrm{BF}_U\;:=\;\frac{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\,\mathrm{RR}_{UD}}{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1},
$$ {#eq-qba-bf}
and the bound is sharp: for every pair $(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})$ with both values at least $1$
there is a confounder configuration attaining equality.
:::

::: {.proof}
*The bias factor as a ratio of weighted averages.* Because $U$ carries all the confounding, the
counterfactual risk had the exposed arm been left unexposed is, by standardization over the exposed
confounder distribution, $\sum_u p_0(u)f_1(u)$. Hence the causal risk ratio for the effect on the exposed
is $\big(\sum_u p_1(u)f_1(u)\big)\big/\big(\sum_u p_0(u)f_1(u)\big)$, while the observed risk ratio is
$\big(\sum_u p_1(u)f_1(u)\big)\big/\big(\sum_u p_0(u)f_0(u)\big)$. Dividing, the common numerator
cancels and
$$
B=\frac{\sum_{u}p_0(u)f_1(u)}{\sum_{u}p_0(u)f_0(u)}
=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{f_1}[\,p_0(U)\,]}{\mathbb{E}_{f_0}[\,p_0(U)\,]}.
$$ {#eq-qba-b-ratio}
The bias factor is the ratio of the unexposed-risk function averaged over the two confounder
distributions.

*Reduction to a box.* Both $B$ and the constraints are invariant to multiplying $p_0(\cdot)$ by a positive
constant, so normalize $\min_u p_0(u)=1$; then $p_0(u)\in[1,R]$ for all $u$, where $R:=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$.
Write $S:=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$, so the constraint $\max_u f_1(u)/f_0(u)\le S$ reads $f_1(u)\le S f_0(u)$ for
every $u$. We maximize @eq-qba-b-ratio over $p_0\in[1,R]^{\mathcal{U}}$ and over probability vectors
$f_1,f_0$ obeying this pointwise constraint.

*Maximizing over $p_0$: the optimum is at a vertex.* Fix $f_1,f_0$ and vary a single coordinate
$t=p_0(u)\in[1,R]$, holding the others fixed. Writing $a,b>0$ for the partial sums over the other
coordinates, $B(t)=\big(a+f_1(u)\,t\big)\big/\big(b+f_0(u)\,t\big)$, whose derivative
$B'(t)=\big(f_1(u)\,b-f_0(u)\,a\big)\big/\big(b+f_0(u)\,t\big)^2$ has a sign independent of $t$: a ratio of
two affine functions of $t$ is monotone across the whole interval, since the numerator of $B'(t)$ never
changes sign. A function monotone in each coordinate separately attains its maximum over the box
$[1,R]^{\mathcal{U}}$ at a vertex, because moving any single coordinate toward its better endpoint never
lowers $B$, so no interior point can be optimal; hence the optimum has every $p_0(u)\in\{1,R\}$, and
coordinate ascent reaches it.

*The two-cell reduction.* At such a vertex, partition $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_R\sqcup\mathcal{U}_1$ with
$p_0=R$ on $\mathcal{U}_R$ and $p_0=1$ on $\mathcal{U}_1$. Put $a=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_R}f_1(u)$ and
$b=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_R}f_0(u)$, the masses the two confounder distributions place on the high-risk
set. Then $\sum_u p_0(u)f_1(u)=R\,a+(1-a)=1+(R-1)a$ and likewise the denominator is $1+(R-1)b$, so
$$
B=\frac{1+(R-1)a}{1+(R-1)b}.
$$ {#eq-qba-b-ab}
This is increasing in $a$ and decreasing in $b$. The pointwise constraint gives
$a=\sum_{\mathcal{U}_R}f_1\le S\sum_{\mathcal{U}_R}f_0=S\,b$, and of course $a\le 1$; so for fixed $b$ the
largest feasible $a$ is $\min(1,S b)$.

*Optimizing the two cells.* If $Sb\le 1$, set $a=Sb$; then
$B=\big(1+(R-1)Sb\big)\big/\big(1+(R-1)b\big)=:g(b)$, and the numerator of $g'(b)$ is
$$
(R-1)S\big(1+(R-1)b\big)-\big(1+(R-1)Sb\big)(R-1)
=(R-1)\big[S+S(R-1)b-1-(R-1)Sb\big]=(R-1)(S-1)\ge 0,
$$
where the two middle terms $S(R-1)b$ and $(R-1)Sb$ cancel; so $g$ increases and we push $b$ up to the
regime boundary $Sb=1$, that is $b=1/S$ with $a=1$. If instead $Sb>1$, then $a=1$ and
$B=R\big/\big(1+(R-1)b\big)$ decreases in $b$, so we push $b$ down to the same boundary $b=1/S$. Either
way the maximum is at $a=1$, $b=1/S$, giving
$$
B^{\star}=\frac{1+(R-1)}{1+(R-1)/S}=\frac{R}{(S+R-1)/S}=\frac{RS}{R+S-1}
=\frac{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\,\mathrm{RR}_{UD}}{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1}=\mathrm{BF}_U,
$$
which is @eq-qba-bf.

*Sharpness.* The optimizing configuration is realizable with a two-point confounder
$\mathcal{U}=\{0,1\}$: take $p_0(0)=1$, $p_0(1)=R$, put all of the exposed mass on the high-risk level,
$f_1(1)=1$, and split the unexposed mass as $f_0(1)=1/S$, $f_0(0)=1-1/S$, which satisfies
$f_1(1)/f_0(1)=S$ and $f_1(0)/f_0(0)=0\le S$. Substituting into @eq-qba-b-ratio returns $B=\mathrm{BF}_U$
exactly, so no smaller bound is possible. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why sharpness, not just validity, matters.** Many sensitivity bounds are merely *valid*: the true bias is
no larger than the bound. Sharpness says more, that the bound is *attained* by an actual confounder
configuration, so it cannot be improved. This is what lets the E-value be an *exact* threshold rather than a
conservative guess. A valid but loose bound would overstate how much confounding is needed and so overstate
robustness; a bound that is attained means "an association of exactly the stated size on both legs is
enough, and nothing weaker is", which is the precise claim a reader can act on. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The bound depends on the data only through the two sensitivity parameters, and it is symmetric in them:
$\mathrm{BF}_U$ is unchanged under $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\leftrightarrow\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$. The E-value is the
point on the curve $\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ where the two parameters are equal.

::: {#thm-evalue-derivation}
## The E-value and its minimality
Let $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}>1$ be an observed risk ratio (for a protective effect
$\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}<1$, replace it by $1/\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ throughout). Define the
**E-value**
$$
E\;=\;\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}+\sqrt{\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,(\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}-1)}.
$$ {#eq-qba-evalue}
Then:

1. Unmeasured confounding can fully explain the observed association away (reduce the true risk ratio to
the null) only if the two sensitivity parameters satisfy
$\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\mathrm{RR}_{UD}/(\mathrm{RR}_{EU}+\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)\ge\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$.

2. Setting $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E$ achieves equality $\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$,
and $E$ is the smallest common value with this property.

3. $E$ is minimal in the strong sense that if *both* sensitivity parameters are strictly below $E$ then
$\mathrm{BF}_U<\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, so the result cannot be explained away: at least one of
$\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ must be at least $E$.

Moreover $E\ge 1$, with $E=1$ iff $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1$, and $E$ is strictly increasing in
$\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, so a larger observed effect is harder to explain away.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Write $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{true}}\cdot B$ with $B$ the confounding
bias factor. "Explaining away" means $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{true}}\le 1$, i.e. $B\ge\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$.
By @lem-qba-sharp-bound the largest bias factor attainable with sensitivity parameters
$(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})$ is $\mathrm{BF}_U$, so such a $B$ exists only if
$\mathrm{BF}_U\ge\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$.

*Part 2.* On the diagonal $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=v\ge 1$,
$\mathrm{BF}_U(v,v)=v^2/(2v-1)$. Setting this equal to $\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=:\rho$ gives
$v^2=\rho(2v-1)$, i.e. the quadratic $v^2-2\rho v+\rho=0$, whose roots are
$v=\rho\pm\sqrt{\rho^2-\rho}=\rho\pm\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}$. The smaller root is below $1$ for $\rho>1$
(at $\rho=2$ it equals $2-\sqrt2\approx0.586$), hence infeasible: $v$ is a common value of the two
sensitivity parameters, which are risk ratios of associations and so are at least $1$ by construction
(@eq-qba-sensitivity-params), forcing $v\ge1$; the admissible root is the
larger one, $E=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}$, which is @eq-qba-evalue. To see $E$ is the smallest common value
giving $\mathrm{BF}_U\ge\rho$, note $\psi(v):=v^2/(2v-1)$ has derivative
$\psi'(v)=\big(2v(2v-1)-2v^2\big)/(2v-1)^2=2v(v-1)/(2v-1)^2\ge 0$ for $v\ge1$, so $\psi$ is increasing;
thus $\mathrm{BF}_U(v,v)=\psi(v)\ge\rho$ holds exactly for $v\ge E$.

*Part 3.* The bias factor is increasing in each argument: with $x=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$, $y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$,
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{xy}{x+y-1}=\frac{y(x+y-1)-xy}{(x+y-1)^2}=\frac{y(y-1)}{(x+y-1)^2}\ge0,
$$
and symmetrically in $y$. Hence if $x<E$ and $y<E$ then
$\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)<\mathrm{BF}_U(E,E)=\rho=\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, contradicting Part 1; so at least
one parameter is $\ge E$. Finally $E(\rho)=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}$ has $E(1)=1$ and
$E'(\rho)=1+\frac{2\rho-1}{2\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}}>0$ for $\rho>1$, so $E\ge1$ with equality iff $\rho=1$,
and $E$ strictly increases in $\rho$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and a feel for the formula.** The E-value converts an estimate into a robustness score
on the same scale a clinician already uses for risk ratios, which is why it travels well into an HTA report
and why it now appears routinely alongside NMA and ITC estimates. A quick numerical anchor: for an observed
$\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}=2$, $E=2+\sqrt{2\cdot 1}=2+\sqrt2\approx 3.41$, so confounding would need a
risk-ratio strength above $3.4$ on *both* legs to erase a doubling of risk. The shape
$E=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}$ repays reading: near the null ($\rho\to 1^{+}$) it behaves like
$1+\sqrt{\rho-1}$, rising as the *square root* of the excess, so a barely significant estimate has an
E-value only a little above $1$ and is easy to explain away; for large $\rho$ it grows like $2\rho$, so
strong estimates demand proportionally strong confounding. For our COPD running example the plug-in effect
is $\mathrm{RR}=0.50$, giving $E\approx 3.44$ (computed in @sec-qba-example); an unreported prognostic
difference weaker than a $3.4$-fold association on each leg cannot overturn it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading and reporting the E-value.** The E-value translates a point estimate into a single
interpretable number: *an unmeasured confounder (or, in the ITC setting below, an unmeasured effect
modifier) would have to be associated with both the treatment assignment and the outcome by a risk ratio
of at least $E$, beyond the measured covariates, to explain the observed effect away; anything weaker
cannot.* A large $E$ signals a robust finding, a small one a fragile finding. One also reports the E-value
of the confidence-interval limit nearest the null, computed by @eq-qba-evalue with
$\mathrm{RR}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ replaced by that limit (and equal to $1$ when the interval already includes
the null): it is the strength of confounding needed to shift the interval to touch the null. The E-value
is a property of the estimate alone, requiring no specification of the bias parameters; that economy is
its appeal and also its limitation, since it is silent on whether confounding of strength $E$ is
*plausible*. The general bound was established by Ding and VanderWeele and popularized as the E-value by
@vanderweele2017evalue; the same $\mathrm{BF}_U$ bounds the bias for total-population standardization, not
only the effect-on-treated standardization we proved. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Mind the scale: the E-value lives on the risk-ratio scale.** Formula @eq-qba-evalue takes a *risk ratio*.
Feeding it a log odds ratio, or an odds ratio for a common outcome, is a common and consequential misuse.
Convert first. The practical rules, with the approximate conversions of @vanderweele2017evalue, are
collected here.

| Reported effect | Convert to a risk ratio by | Then |
|---|---|---|
| risk ratio | nothing, it already is one | apply @eq-qba-evalue |
| odds ratio, rare outcome | $\mathrm{RR}\approx\mathrm{OR}$ | apply @eq-qba-evalue to the OR |
| odds ratio, common outcome | $\mathrm{RR}\approx\sqrt{\mathrm{OR}}$ | apply @eq-qba-evalue to $\sqrt{\mathrm{OR}}$ |
| hazard ratio, rare outcome | $\mathrm{RR}\approx\mathrm{HR}$ | apply @eq-qba-evalue to the HR |
| hazard ratio, common outcome | approximate conversion of @vanderweele2017evalue | apply @eq-qba-evalue to the converted value |
| risk difference, mean difference, RMST difference | no ratio-scale E-value exists | use the tipping point (@sec-qba-tipping) instead |

For a protective effect ($\mathrm{RR}<1$) convert to $1/\mathrm{RR}$ first, as in the theorem. The running
example works on the log-risk-ratio scale, so no conversion is needed there; a survival endpoint reported
as a hazard ratio would use one of the hazard-ratio rows. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The indirect-comparison E-value {#sec-qba-itc-evalue}

In a classical observational study both sensitivity parameters in @eq-qba-sensitivity-params are unknown,
and the symmetric E-value is the natural summary. An unanchored indirect comparison is different in a way
that can be exploited. The covariate that threatens the comparison, an effect modifier
(@def-effect-modifier) that is imbalanced between the IPD and comparator populations and is *unreported*
by the comparator, is nonetheless **observed in the analyst's own IPD**. Its association with the outcome
is therefore estimable from the IPD outcome model, even though its distribution in the comparator
population is not. One of the two arms of the bias factor becomes known data rather than an assumed
sensitivity parameter, and the E-value sharpens accordingly.

The map from the classical confounding picture to the indirect-comparison picture is worth pinning down,
because every symbol in the E-value derivation keeps its algebra but changes its clinical referent.

| Classical confounding (@sec-qba-evalue) | Unanchored ITC (this section) |
|---|---|
| exposure $A\in\{0,1\}$ | trial-population membership: IPD population versus comparator population |
| the exposed arm | the IPD (index-treatment) population |
| the unexposed arm | the comparator population |
| unmeasured confounder $U$ | the covariate the comparator did not report |
| $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$, imbalance of $U$ across exposure | imbalance of the covariate across the two trial populations |
| $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, association of $U$ with the outcome | covariate-outcome association, *estimable from the IPD model* |
| both arms of the bias factor unknown | one arm ($\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$) is known data; only the imbalance is assumed |

The last row is the whole point: half of the sensitivity problem is estimated rather than guessed.

We set the stage with the unanchored estimand of Chapter 17. The IPD study fits an outcome model
$g\big(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid \mathbf{x},u]\big)=\beta_0+\boldsymbol{\beta}_R^{\top}\mathbf{x}+\beta_U u$ on the
reported covariates $\mathbf{x}$ and the unreported covariate $U$. The comparator-population effect of the
index treatment against the comparator, on the analysis scale, is the g-computation contrast
$$
\Delta=g\!\left(\int g^{-1}\!\big(\beta_0+\boldsymbol{\beta}_R^{\top}\mathbf{x}+\beta_U u\big)\,
dF_0(\mathbf{x},u)\right)-g(\mu_0),
$$ {#eq-qba-unanchored-estimand}
where $F_0$ is the comparator covariate distribution and $\mu_0$ its reported outcome under the comparator
treatment. In words, reading @eq-qba-unanchored-estimand from the inside out: take the IPD outcome model,
predict each comparator patient's risk *as if they had received the index treatment* from their covariates
$(\mathbf{x},u)$, average those predicted risks over the comparator population $F_0$, transform that average
back to the analysis scale with $g$, and subtract the comparator's own reported outcome $g(\mu_0)$. The
result is what the index-versus-comparator contrast would be in the comparator population. The bias from
omitting $U$ is the gap between $\Delta$ computed with $U$ held at the analyst's
best guess (its IPD value) and $\Delta$ computed at $U$'s true, unknown comparator value. On the
risk-ratio scale this bias is a bias factor, and the question of the E-value is how large the across-arm
imbalance of $U$ must be to produce it, *given* that $U$'s outcome association is pinned down by the IPD.

Two things need saying before the definition. First, what "$\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$" means: it is not
the treatment effect but the *amount of bias that would have to be present to nullify it*, read on the ratio
scale. If the adjusted risk ratio is $0.50$, explaining it away means multiplying it back up to $1$, a
factor of $2$; so $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1/0.50=2.0$, and in general
$\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\exp(|\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}|)$, where $\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}$ is the log-scale
adjusted effect with the unreported covariate held at its IPD value. "Held at its IPD value" means the
comparator population is given the covariate's IPD distribution as a best guess, so $\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}$
is the plug-in adjusted effect, not the covariate's raw mean. Second, why the formula has three cases: with
the outcome association fixed at $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, the bias factor can never exceed $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ no
matter how extreme the imbalance (proved as @prp-itc-evalue below), so the equation
$\mathrm{BF}_U=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ has a finite solution only when
$\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$; that ceiling is what splits the definition into its three
branches.

::: {#def-itc-evalue}
## The indirect-comparison E-value
Consider an unanchored indirect comparison on a ratio scale (binary or count outcome). Let
$\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\ge 1$ be the observed bias factor, the ratio-scale magnitude
$\exp(|\Delta_{\mathrm{IPD}}|)$ of the adjusted effect @eq-qba-unanchored-estimand evaluated with the
unreported covariate held at its IPD value, and let
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)\ge 1$ be the IPD-estimated association of the unreported covariate $U$
with the outcome, conditional on the reported covariates. The **indirect-comparison E-value** is the
minimum across-arm association $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$ that the unreported covariate must have, given
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, to produce a bias factor as large as $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$:
$$
E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=
\begin{cases}
1, & \mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\le 1,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}},
& 1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD},\\[8pt]
+\infty, & \mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-qba-itc-evalue}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the three cases.** The indirect-comparison E-value answers one question, "how imbalanced would the
unreported covariate have to be, across the two trial populations, to overturn the result, given how
strongly the IPD says it acts on the outcome?", and its three cases are three honest answers. If
$\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}\le 1$ the estimate already sits at or past the null and no bias is needed, so
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=1$. If $1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ a finite imbalance suffices, and the
formula returns exactly how much. If $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ the covariate is too
weakly prognostic to matter: *no* imbalance, however extreme, can manufacture enough bias, and
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty$ certifies the result robust to this covariate. The word "infinite" here does not
mean "no bias exists"; it means "no across-arm imbalance in *this one covariate* can explain the result
away, under the single-covariate bias-factor model, with $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ treated as fixed." That
narrower claim is exactly what a dossier can defend. For the running example the IPD gives
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=1.65$, below the needed $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=2.01$, so we land in the third case and
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty$ (computed in @sec-qba-example). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The three cases, and in particular the infinite case that the symmetric E-value can never deliver, follow
from the same sharp bound.

::: {#prp-itc-evalue}
## Derivation and the robustness certificate
With $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ as in @def-itc-evalue:

1. If $1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, the value @eq-qba-itc-evalue is the unique
$\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$ solving $\mathrm{BF}_U(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, and
it exceeds $1$.

2. The maximum bias factor achievable by *any* finite across-arm imbalance, with the outcome association
fixed at $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, is $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ itself:
$\lim_{\mathrm{RR}_{EU}\to\infty}\mathrm{BF}_U(\mathrm{RR}_{EU},\mathrm{RR}_{UD})=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, the
limit being approached from below and monotonically. Consequently, if
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, no across-arm imbalance can overturn the result under the
single-covariate bias model, and $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty$ is a provable robustness certificate.

3. When the IPD-estimated outcome association happens to equal the symmetric E-value,
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E$ with $E$ from @eq-qba-evalue applied to $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, the
indirect-comparison E-value coincides with it, $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=E$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Solve $\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y-1}=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ for $x=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$
with $y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ fixed. Cross-multiplying, $xy=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(x+y-1)$, hence
$x\,(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y-1)$ and
$x=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y-1)/(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})$, which is @eq-qba-itc-evalue. When
$1<\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}<y$ the denominator is positive and $x>0$; moreover
$x-1=\big(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y-1)-(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})\big)/(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})
=(y-1)(\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}-1)/(y-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}})>0$, so $x>1$. Uniqueness is immediate
since $\mathrm{BF}_U(\cdot,y)$ is strictly increasing in its first argument (Part 3 of
@thm-evalue-derivation).

*Part 2.* For fixed $y>1$,
$\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y-1}=\dfrac{y}{1+(y-1)/x}\uparrow y$ as $x\to\infty$, monotonically since
$(y-1)/x$ decreases. Thus the achievable bias factor is bounded above by $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$. If
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ the target is unreachable for every finite imbalance, so
the minimal sufficient $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$ is $+\infty$ by convention, and the result cannot be explained
away by imbalance in $U$ alone no matter how extreme; this is the certificate. (Algebraically, the
formula @eq-qba-itc-evalue has a nonpositive denominator here, confirming no finite solution.)

*Part 3.* If $y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=E$ then, by Part 2 of @thm-evalue-derivation,
$\mathrm{BF}_U(E,E)=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, so $x=E$ already solves the equation; by uniqueness
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=E$. $\square$
:::

::: {#cor-itc-evalue-monotone}
## The indirect-comparison E-value against the symmetric one
Fix an observed bias factor $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\rho>1$ and regard $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}$ as a function
of the IPD-estimated outcome association $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=y$. On the finite range $y>\rho$ the map
$y\mapsto E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)=\rho(y-1)/(y-\rho)$ is strictly decreasing, with $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)\to+\infty$
as $y\downarrow\rho$ and $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)\to\rho$ as $y\to\infty$. It crosses the symmetric E-value
$E=\rho+\sqrt{\rho(\rho-1)}$ exactly at $y=E$: for $\rho<y<E$ it exceeds $E$, and for $y>E$ it is smaller
than $E$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Differentiating,
$$
\frac{d}{dy}\,\frac{\rho(y-1)}{y-\rho}
=\rho\,\frac{(y-\rho)-(y-1)}{(y-\rho)^2}
=\frac{\rho(1-\rho)}{(y-\rho)^2}<0
\quad\text{for }\rho>1,
$$
so $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}$ strictly decreases on $y>\rho$. The two limits are immediate from the rational form:
as $y\downarrow\rho$ the denominator $\to 0^{+}$ with positive numerator, and as $y\to\infty$ the ratio
$\rho(y-1)/(y-\rho)\to\rho$. By @prp-itc-evalue(3), $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(E)=E$; strict monotonicity then forces
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)>E$ for $\rho<y<E$ and $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}(y)<E$ for $y>E$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What "sharper" does and does not mean.** It is tempting to say the indirect-comparison E-value is "always
larger because it uses more information"; @cor-itc-evalue-monotone shows that is false. The ITC E-value is
*better calibrated*, not uniformly larger: by plugging in the known $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ it can land above or
below the symmetric E-value. A weakly prognostic unreported covariate ($y<E$, and especially $y\le\rho$) is
*harder or impossible* to weaponize, so more imbalance would be required and $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}>E$; a
strongly prognostic one ($y>E$) needs *less* imbalance to do damage, so $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}<E$. Using the data
can cut either way, and that honest calibration, not a guaranteed increase, is the gain. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this is the honest summary for an unmeasured effect modifier.** The infinite case has no analogue
in the classical E-value, where both arms are unknown and the bias factor can be pushed arbitrarily high
by sending both to infinity. Here one arm is data. If the IPD says $U$ is only weakly prognostic
($\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ small), then even a wildly imbalanced $U$ cannot manufacture a large bias, and the
unanchored comparison is robust to it whatever the comparator distribution turns out to be. This is
exactly the residual-bias question raised by @thm-sema-insufficient, now answered quantitatively for one
covariate at a time. Three caveats must travel with the number, all visible in the derivation: it treats
the IPD-estimated $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=\exp(|\beta_U|)$ as fixed, propagating none of that estimate's
sampling uncertainty; it is a single-covariate bias-factor argument, so several jointly imbalanced
covariates require the multivariate analysis of @sec-qba-norta; and it is a ratio-scale quantity, defined
for binary and count outcomes, not for continuous or time-to-event effects, for which the tipping-point
analysis of @sec-qba-tipping is the appropriate instrument. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## NORTA: imputing the unreported covariate distribution {#sec-qba-norta}

Before any formulas, the practical problem NORTA solves. The comparator publication gives you a few
*margins*: the distribution of each covariate on its own, usually just a mean and a standard deviation (age
is $62\pm 9$ years, say) or a prevalence ($30\%$ are current smokers). A margin says nothing about how two
covariates move *together* in that population, their *dependence* (do older patients tend to have worse lung
function?). To recompute the adjusted effect you need the full joint distribution of all covariates in the
comparator population, and you are missing two things: the margin of the *unreported* covariate, which you
must assume, and *all* of the dependence, which the comparator never reports. NORTA fills both gaps in a
disciplined way. You supply the assumed margins, and you borrow the dependence from the one place it is
observed, your own IPD. The name is literal, *normal to anything*: start from correlated normal draws,
which carry the borrowed dependence, then reshape each coordinate into the margin you want. The rest of this
section makes "reshape" and "borrow the dependence" precise and flags that borrowing as the method's key
assumption.

The E-value summarizes the threat of a single unmeasured covariate without ever simulating it. To go
further, to actually recompute the adjusted effect @eq-qba-unanchored-estimand under an assumption about
the unreported covariate, we must construct a comparator-population covariate distribution that (i) honors
every reported marginal summary, (ii) places a chosen marginal on the unreported covariate, and (iii)
carries a credible dependence structure linking them. Aggregate comparator data fix the margins but say
nothing about the dependence (Sklar's theorem, @thm-sklar, makes this precise: the margins and the copula
are separately specifiable). The only place the dependence is observed is the IPD. The **NORTA**
(normal-to-anything) construction supplies exactly this: it glues the target margins to a Gaussian copula
(@def-gaussian-copula) whose correlation is borrowed from the IPD.

::: {#thm-norta-copula}
## The NORTA construction
Let $F_1,\dots,F_d$ be target univariate distribution functions, with generalized inverses
$F_j^{-1}$, and let $\boldsymbol{\Omega}\succeq 0$ be a correlation matrix (symmetric, unit diagonal).
Draw $\mathbf{Z}=(Z_1,\dots,Z_d)\sim\mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$ and set
$$
X_j\;=\;F_j^{-1}\!\big(\Phi(Z_j)\big),\qquad j=1,\dots,d,
$$ {#eq-qba-norta}
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. Then:

1. **(Exact margins.)** For every target $F_j$, discrete or continuous, $X_j\sim F_j$.

2. **(Induced copula.)** If in addition every $F_j$ is continuous, the joint distribution function of
$\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ is
$$
F_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big),
$$ {#eq-qba-norta-joint}
so $\mathbf{X}$ has margins $F_1,\dots,F_d$ and Gaussian copula $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$; by uniqueness
in Sklar's theorem $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ is the unique copula of $\mathbf{X}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Since $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ has unit diagonal, each $Z_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and $\Phi$ is
continuous, so by the probability integral transform (@thm-inverse-cdf, part 2) the variable
$U_j:=\Phi(Z_j)$ is uniform on $(0,1)$. By the inverse-transform property (@thm-inverse-cdf, part 1),
$F_j^{-1}(U_j)\sim F_j$ for any distribution function $F_j$. Hence $X_j=F_j^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))\sim F_j$,
with no continuity required.

*Part 2.* Let $U_j=\Phi(Z_j)$ as above; by @prp-gaussian-copula-is-copula the vector
$(U_1,\dots,U_d)$ has joint distribution function exactly the Gaussian copula
$C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. The defining equivalence of a generalized inverse, $\{F_j^{-1}(u)\le x\}=\{u\le
F_j(x)\}$ (the Galois inequality @eq-qmc-galois, used in @thm-inverse-cdf), gives for each coordinate
$\{X_j\le x_j\}=\{F_j^{-1}(U_j)\le x_j\}=\{U_j\le F_j(x_j)\}$. Intersecting over $j$,
$$
F_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x})=P\Big(\bigcap_{j=1}^{d}\{X_j\le x_j\}\Big)
=P\Big(\bigcap_{j=1}^{d}\{U_j\le F_j(x_j)\}\Big)
=C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big),
$$
which is @eq-qba-norta-joint. With continuous margins, Sklar's theorem (@thm-sklar) says the copula in the
factorization $F_{\mathbf{X}}=C(F_1,\dots,F_d)$ is unique, and we have exhibited it as
$C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation.** @thm-norta-copula is the guarantee that the recipe does what the introduction
promised. Part 1 says the simulated covariates land on *exactly* the margins you asked for (the assumed
prevalence or mean is honored, discrete or continuous). Part 2 says the dependence you wired in through
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ comes out as *exactly* a Gaussian copula, with nothing sneaking in from the marginal
reshaping. So you may choose margins and dependence separately and trust that both emerge as specified,
which is what makes NORTA a reliable comparator-population generator. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The construction is exact for the margins but leaves one question open: how to choose $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$
so that the simulated population reproduces the dependence seen in the IPD. The natural target is the rank
correlation, because it is what survives the marginal transforms and because it is invariant to the choice
of margins.

::: {#lem-qba-spearman-matching}
## Spearman matching for the Gaussian copula
Let $(X_j,X_k)$ be constructed by @eq-qba-norta with continuous margins and Gaussian-copula correlation
$\Omega_{jk}=\rho^{N}$. Then:

1. Spearman's rank correlation $\rho^{S}(X_j,X_k)$ depends only on the copula $C_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$,
not on the margins $F_j,F_k$; it equals $\rho^{S}(Z_j,Z_k)$.

2. For the bivariate Gaussian copula, $\rho^{S}=\frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho^{N}/2)$. Hence choosing
$$
\rho^{N}=2\sin\!\big(\pi\,\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}/6\big)
$$ {#eq-qba-spearman-transform}
makes the simulated Spearman correlation equal the IPD Spearman correlation $\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}$
exactly.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Spearman's rho is the Pearson correlation of the probability-integral transforms,
$\rho^{S}(X_j,X_k)=\operatorname{corr}\!\big(F_j(X_j),F_k(X_k)\big)$. For continuous margins,
$F_j(X_j)=F_j\big(F_j^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))\big)=\Phi(Z_j)$, since $F_j\circ F_j^{-1}$ is the identity on the
range of a continuous $F_j$. The map $\Phi$ is strictly increasing, so
$\operatorname{corr}(\Phi(Z_j),\Phi(Z_k))$ is a functional of the joint law of $(Z_j,Z_k)$ alone, hence
of the copula; it does not involve $F_j,F_k$. This proves the invariance and the identity
$\rho^{S}(X_j,X_k)=\rho^{S}(Z_j,Z_k)$.

*Part 2.* The identity $\rho^{S}=\frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho^{N}/2)$ for a bivariate normal with correlation
$\rho^{N}$ is the classical "arcsine law" for the grade correlation of the Gaussian copula; we take it as
a known property of the bivariate normal (see the Notes). Inverting,
$\rho^{N}=2\sin(\pi\rho^{S}/6)$, which is @eq-qba-spearman-transform; feeding the IPD value
$\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}$ on the right reproduces it as the simulated Spearman correlation by Part 1.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why rank correlation, and the discrete and definiteness caveats.** The Pearson correlation of
$(X_j,X_k)$ produced by @eq-qba-norta is in general *not* $\Omega_{jk}$: the nonlinear marginal transforms
$F_j^{-1}\circ\Phi$ distort linear correlation, and the distortion depends on the margins. Rank
correlation is the right invariant precisely because, by @lem-qba-spearman-matching, it passes through the
transforms untouched, which is why the implementation borrows the IPD's *Spearman* matrix and maps it by
@eq-qba-spearman-transform. Two practical points. First, for a binary covariate (the unreported $U$ is
often binary) the margin is discrete, so @lem-qba-spearman-matching is approximate: the transform
$F_j(X_j)$ is no longer exactly uniform (@thm-inverse-cdf, part 2 fails for discrete $F$), and the
induced copula in @thm-norta-copula is one of the many copulas Sklar's theorem allows rather than a unique
one. The marginal-recovery guarantee (part 1) still holds exactly. Second, the element-wise transform
@eq-qba-spearman-transform applied to an empirical Spearman matrix need not return a positive semidefinite
matrix, so before constructing the copula one projects it onto the nearest correlation matrix (symmetrize,
floor the eigenvalues at a small positive value, and rescale to unit diagonal). Both adjustments are
benign and standard. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What actually changes when $U$ is binary, and how much to trust the borrowed correlation.** Two applied
points, since the unreported covariate is often a binary flag (a biomarker-positive indicator, a smoking
status). First, the discrete caveat above is narrow in its consequences. Marginal recovery stays *exact*: if
you assume a comparator prevalence of $30\%$, the simulated population has prevalence $30\%$, full stop. What
becomes approximate is only the *dependence*: the Spearman match @eq-qba-spearman-transform no longer lands
the simulated rank correlation exactly on the IPD value, and the copula is no longer unique. In practice
this perturbs the induced covariate correlations slightly, and hence the adjusted effect slightly, but it
never distorts the assumed prevalence, which is usually the very quantity the sensitivity analysis is
sweeping. Second, borrowing the IPD dependence is a *substantive* assumption, not a technical convenience:
it asserts that age and lung function (say) hang together in the comparator population the way they do in
your trial. When that is doubtful, the honest move is to redo the analysis under a few alternative
correlation matrices (including independence and a strong correlation of each sign) and report the range. If
the conclusion is stable across them the borrowing did no harm; if it is not, the dependence itself has
become a bias parameter deserving its own sensitivity sweep. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

With the comparator covariate population in hand, the deterministic ITC bias analysis is a sweep:
choose a grid of assumed marginals for the unreported covariate, and for each one simulate the comparator
population by @eq-qba-norta, marginalize the IPD outcome model over it, and record the adjusted effect
@eq-qba-unanchored-estimand. The resulting curve is the input to the tipping-point and probabilistic
analyses.

::: {#exm-qba-norta-correlated}
## NORTA with a borrowed dependence, in closed form
The worked example of @sec-qba-example takes the comparator covariates independent, which makes NORTA
invisible; here we let NORTA do its job so the dependence is seen to bite. Keep the running COPD model
$\log P(Y=1\mid x_R,u)=\beta_0+\beta_R x_R+\beta_U u$ with $\beta_R=0.4$, $\beta_U=-0.5$, normal margins
$x_R\sim\mathcal{N}(1.0,0.5^2)$ (age) and $u\sim\mathcal{N}(2.0,1.0^2)$ ($\mathrm{FEV}_1$), and comparator
risk $\mu_0=0.47$. Suppose the IPD reports a Spearman rank correlation between age and $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ of
$\rho^{S}_{\mathrm{IPD}}=-0.3$ (older patients tend to have worse lung function). NORTA borrows it through
@eq-qba-spearman-transform: the Gaussian-copula correlation is
$$
\rho^{N}=2\sin\!\big(\pi\,(-0.3)/6\big)=2\sin(-0.1571)=-0.313.
$$
For normal margins the copula correlation *is* the Pearson correlation, so
$\operatorname{Cov}(x_R,u)=\rho^{N}\sigma_R\sigma_U=-0.313\times 0.5\times 1.0=-0.1564$. The linear
predictor $W=\beta_0+\beta_R x_R+\beta_U u$ is then normal with variance
$$
\operatorname{Var}(W)=\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2+2\beta_R\beta_U\operatorname{Cov}(x_R,u)
=0.04+0.25+2(0.4)(-0.5)(-0.1564)=0.29+0.0626=0.3526,
$$
against $\operatorname{Var}(W)=0.29$ under independence. By the log-normal mean
$\mathbb{E}[e^{W}]=\exp\!\big(\mathbb{E}[W]+\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(W)\big)$, the dependence adds
$\tfrac12(0.3526-0.29)=0.0313$ to the log risk, so the adjusted log-risk-ratio moves from $-0.700$ (the
independence value of @sec-qba-example) to $-0.700+0.0313=-0.669$, a risk ratio of $e^{-0.669}=0.512$
instead of $0.497$. Borrowing a realistic negative age-lung-function dependence nudges the estimate about
$3\%$ toward the null; a positive borrowed correlation would push it the other way. That shift, invisible to
the margins alone, is exactly the information NORTA imports from the IPD. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Tipping-point analysis {#sec-qba-tipping}

A sensitivity curve answers "what if the unreported mean were such-and-such?" The tipping point distills
the curve to its single decision-relevant value: the assumed marginal of the unreported covariate at
which the conclusion changes.

::: {#def-tipping-point}
## Tipping point
Let $m\mapsto\Delta(m)$ be the **sensitivity curve** that maps an assumed comparator marginal $m$ of the
unreported covariate $U$ (its mean for a continuous covariate, its prevalence for a binary one) to the
adjusted effect @eq-qba-unanchored-estimand on the analysis scale, all other inputs held fixed. Fix a
**decision threshold** $c$ (the null value, $c=0$ on a log-ratio or difference scale, by default). A
**tipping point** is a value $m^{\dagger}$ with
$$
\Delta(m^{\dagger})=c.
$$ {#eq-qba-tipping}
The **tipping gap** is $m^{\dagger}-\bar{x}_{U}$, the signed distance from the value $\bar{x}_U$ the
covariate takes in the IPD. Given a **plausible range** $[m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]$ for the
comparator marginal, the conclusion is flagged **fragile** if $m^{\dagger}\in[m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]$,
since a believable comparator value would reverse it, and **robust** if $m^{\dagger}$ lies outside the
range. One may report the tipping point of the confidence limit nearest the threshold in place of the
point estimate. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation.** The tipping point is the sensitivity analysis a clinician can argue about
directly, because it speaks in the covariate's own units. It says: *the conclusion holds unless the
comparator's true mean* $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ *(or prevalence, for a binary covariate) is as extreme as*
$m^{\dagger}$. You then ask a subject-matter question, not a statistical one: is $m^{\dagger}$ inside the
range of values the comparator population could plausibly have? If yes, the result is fragile; if no, it is
robust. The tipping *gap* $m^{\dagger}-\bar{x}_U$ measures how far the comparator would have to differ from
your IPD before the story changes. For the running example this comes out at $m^{\dagger}=0.6$ liters,
against an IPD mean of $2.0$ (see @sec-qba-example). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

For the tipping point to be a well-defined single number we need the sensitivity curve to be monotone, so
that it crosses the threshold at most once. The next proposition shows monotonicity holds under the
natural structural assumptions, via a coupling argument that fixes the copula draws and moves only the
unreported margin.

::: {#prp-qba-tipping-monotone}
## Monotonicity and existence of the tipping point
Suppose the unreported covariate enters the IPD outcome model through a single term $\beta_U u$ with
$\beta_U\neq 0$, the link $g$ is continuous and strictly monotone (so $g^{-1}$ is monotone), and the
assumed marginal family $\{F_{U,m}\}$ is ordered by first-order stochastic dominance in $m$ through a
quantile function $F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)$ that is nondecreasing in $m$ for each $t\in(0,1)$ (as for a location
family, where $F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)=m+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(t)$, or a Bernoulli family, where
$F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{t>1-m\}$). Construct the comparator population by NORTA @eq-qba-norta with a
fixed correlation matrix and fixed reported margins. Then:

1. The sensitivity curve $\Delta(m)$ is monotone in $m$, strictly so where $g^{-1}$ is strictly monotone;
its direction is the sign of $\beta_U$ (composed with the monotonicity of $g$).

2. If the threshold $c$ lies between $\Delta(m_{\mathrm{lo}})$ and $\Delta(m_{\mathrm{hi}})$, a tipping
point $m^{\dagger}\in[m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]$ exists and is unique. If $c$ lies outside the
interval spanned by $\Delta$ over the plausible range, there is no tipping point inside the range and the
conclusion is robust on that range.
:::

The idea behind the proof is simpler than its machinery. If pushing the unreported covariate up always
moves the predicted outcome the same way, because it enters the model through a single term $\beta_U u$ with
a fixed sign, then the sensitivity curve can only go one direction and so crosses any threshold at most
once. The one technical device is a *coupling*: use the *same* normal draws $\mathbf{Z}$ for every assumed
value $m$, changing only the quantile function applied to the last coordinate, so that raising $m$ raises
that covariate for every simulated patient at once and never touches the others. Monotonicity then survives
the averaging over patients.

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* Realize the comparator covariates by the common-$\mathbf{Z}$ coupling of @eq-qba-norta: draw
$\mathbf{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Omega})$ once, set the reported coordinates
$X_{R,j}=F_{R,j}^{-1}(\Phi(Z_j))$ (independent of $m$) and the unreported coordinate
$U(m)=F_{U,m}^{-1}(\Phi(Z_d))$. By hypothesis $F_{U,m}^{-1}(t)$ is nondecreasing in $m$ for each fixed
$t=\Phi(Z_d)$, so for $m\le m'$ we have $U(m)\le U(m')$ pointwise in $\mathbf{Z}$, while $\mathbf{X}_R$ is
unchanged. The linear predictor $\eta(m)=\beta_0+\boldsymbol{\beta}_R^{\top}\mathbf{X}_R+\beta_U U(m)$ is
therefore monotone in $m$ with the sign of $\beta_U$, pointwise in $\mathbf{Z}$, and since $g^{-1}$ is
monotone, the per-subject prediction $g^{-1}(\eta(m))$ is monotone in $m$ pointwise. Taking expectation
over $\mathbf{Z}$ preserves the inequality, so the marginal mean
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Z}}[g^{-1}(\eta(m))]$ is monotone in $m$; applying the monotone $g$ and subtracting
the constant $g(\mu_0)$ leaves $\Delta(m)$ monotone, with strictness inherited wherever $g^{-1}$ is
strictly monotone and $\beta_U\neq0$.

*Part 2.* The curve $\Delta$ is continuous in $m$ (the integrand is continuous in $m$ and bounded by an
integrable envelope, so dominated convergence makes the marginal mean continuous; $g$ is continuous).
A continuous monotone function on $[m_{\mathrm{lo}},m_{\mathrm{hi}}]$ attains the value $c$ exactly once
when $c$ lies between its endpoint values (intermediate value theorem plus injectivity from strict
monotonicity), giving a unique $m^{\dagger}$ in the range; if $c$ is outside the endpoint interval, $\Delta-c$
keeps a constant sign on the range, so no crossing occurs and the sign of the conclusion is constant,
i.e. robust. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Computation and the link to the E-value.** In practice the curve is evaluated on a grid by the NORTA
marginalization of @sec-qba-norta, and the crossing is located by one-dimensional root-finding
(interpolation plus a bracketed solver) on the grid. The tipping point and the indirect-comparison
E-value are two windows onto the same residual bias: the tipping point speaks in the natural units of the
covariate's comparator marginal, which is the most transparent scale for a clinician to judge
plausibility, while $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}$ recasts the same threat as a ratio-scale association. They can give
qualitatively different impressions, since a small tipping gap and a large $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}$ both occur,
and reporting both is the cautious practice. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Probabilistic bias analysis {#sec-qba-probabilistic}

Deterministic analysis commits to a single bias parameter or sweeps a bare grid. Probabilistic bias
analysis instead places a *prior distribution* over the bias parameters and propagates it, separating two
kinds of uncertainty that a single confidence interval conflates: the **systematic** uncertainty from not
knowing the bias parameter, and the ordinary **random** sampling uncertainty.

::: {#def-probabilistic-bias-analysis}
## Probabilistic bias analysis
Let $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b})$ be the QBA correction @eq-qba-correction and let $\pi$ be a
prior on the bias parameter $\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{B}$, encoding external evidence about it. The
**probabilistic bias analysis** draws $\mathbf{b}^{(s)}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\pi$ for
$s=1,\dots,S$, computes the adjusted effects $\theta^{(s)}=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b}^{(s)})$,
and reports two intervals:

- the **systematic interval**, the central $1-\alpha$ empirical quantiles of $\{\theta^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^{S}$,
which captures bias-parameter uncertainty alone;
- the **total interval**, the same quantiles of the *error-perturbed* draws
$\theta_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}=\theta^{(s)}+\varepsilon^{(s)}$ with
$\varepsilon^{(s)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{SE}^2)$ independent draws of the sampling error, which folds
ordinary statistical uncertainty on top.

Draws that violate a structural constraint (a negative reconstructed cell count, an out-of-range
prevalence) are discarded, and the retained fraction is reported. The **probability of benefit** is the
share of draws on the favorable side of the threshold,
$\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}=S^{-1}\sum_s\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(s)}\text{ favorable}\}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Where the prior comes from, and which draws to throw away.** The prior $\pi$ is a sensitivity assumption,
external evidence about the bias parameter, never new data from the trial, and it must be defensible in a
report. Practical defaults: for a continuous comparator mean, center a normal or truncated normal prior at
the IPD value and set its standard deviation to a fraction of the IPD standard deviation (a half or a
third), widening it when the comparator population is known to differ; for a binary comparator prevalence,
elicit a plausible interval from a clinician and fit a Beta prior whose central range matches it (for
instance $\mathrm{Beta}(2,8)$ has mean $0.2$ and most of its mass in $[0.03,0.45]$). Registries, baseline
tables of related trials, and epidemiologic cohorts are the usual sources; when nothing is known, a
deliberately wide prior is the conservative choice. *Invalid draws* are those a prior can produce but the
world cannot: a normal prior on a prevalence can wander below $0$ or above $1$, a drawn covariance can be
incompatible with the fixed margins, a reconstructed cell count can go negative. These are discarded and the
retained fraction reported; a large discard rate is itself a warning that the prior is misspecified. In the
running example the prior is $\mathcal{N}(2.0,0.3^2)$, an IPD-centered normal whose standard deviation is
about a third of the IPD's (see @sec-qba-example). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The two intervals estimate well-defined population quantities, and the Monte Carlo estimates converge to
them; we record this so the procedure is not merely a heuristic.

::: {#thm-qba-pba-convergence}
## Consistency of the probabilistic-bias-analysis intervals
Let $\theta=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b})$ with $\mathbf{b}\sim\pi$ have distribution function
$G_{\mathrm{sys}}$ (the law of the correction under the prior, the *systematic* distribution), and let
$G_{\mathrm{tot}}$ be the law of $\theta+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{SE}^2)$
independent of $\theta$, that is the convolution
$G_{\mathrm{tot}}(t)=\int\Phi\!\big((t-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b}))/\mathrm{SE}\big)\,d\pi(\mathbf{b})$.
As the number of draws $S\to\infty$:

1. The empirical quantiles of $\{\theta^{(s)}\}$ converge almost surely to the quantiles of
$G_{\mathrm{sys}}$ at every continuity point of $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{-1}$; likewise the error-perturbed
quantiles converge to those of $G_{\mathrm{tot}}$.

2. $\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}\to P(\theta\text{ favorable})$ almost surely.

3. $G_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is continuous and strictly increasing wherever $\mathrm{SE}>0$, so its quantiles are
unique and the total interval is well defined for every $\alpha$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* The draws $\theta^{(s)}=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\mathbf{b}^{(s)})$ are independent and
identically distributed with distribution function $G_{\mathrm{sys}}$, so by the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem
the empirical distribution function $\widehat{G}_{S}$ converges to $G_{\mathrm{sys}}$ uniformly, almost
surely. Uniform convergence of distribution functions implies convergence of the corresponding quantile
(generalized inverse) functions at every point where $G_{\mathrm{sys}}^{-1}$ is continuous, which is the
standard quantile-convergence consequence of Glivenko-Cantelli. For the total interval, note
$\theta_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}=\theta^{(s)}+\varepsilon^{(s)}$ are iid with distribution function
$G_{\mathrm{tot}}$ (the independent sum has the stated convolution law), and apply Glivenko-Cantelli
again.

*Part 2.* The indicators $\mathbf{1}\{\theta^{(s)}\text{ favorable}\}$ are iid Bernoulli with mean
$P(\theta\text{ favorable})$ and finite variance, so the strong law of large numbers gives
$\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}\to P(\theta\text{ favorable})$ almost surely.

*Part 3.* For $\mathrm{SE}>0$ the inner map $t\mapsto\Phi((t-\theta_0)/\mathrm{SE})$ is continuous and
strictly increasing for each $\theta_0$, and these properties are preserved under the mixture
$\int(\cdot)\,d\pi$: continuity by dominated convergence (the integrand is bounded by $1$), strict
monotonicity because for $t<t'$ the integrand strictly increases for every $\theta_0$ and the prior
integrates a strictly positive gap to a positive number. Hence $G_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is a continuous, strictly
increasing distribution function, with unique quantiles. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Interpretation.** The systematic interval answers "how much does my conclusion move as the unknown bias
parameter ranges over its prior?"; the total interval answers "and what does ordinary sampling error add
on top?" Their difference is the price of the missing information, isolated from statistical noise; that
separation is the entire point of probabilistic bias analysis (@lash2021qba). In the unanchored ITC the
bias parameter is the comparator marginal of the unreported covariate, the correction
$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{adj}}$ is the NORTA marginalization, and a normal or beta prior on that marginal
yields the two intervals directly. When the sensitivity curve is monotone (@prp-qba-tipping-monotone) the
favorable fraction $\widehat{P}_{\mathrm{ben}}$ is a clean Monte Carlo estimate of the prior probability
that the comparator marginal lies on the favorable side of the tipping point. In the language of the rest
of the book this is the same random-effects logic as a Bayesian NMA (Chapter 15), except the "random"
quantity is not a study effect drawn from a hierarchical prior but the unreported covariate value drawn from
an external prior, and the total interval is its predictive spread folded together with sampling error.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A worked E-value and tipping-point example {#sec-qba-example}

We now carry the running COPD comparison of @exm-qba-running through every instrument of the chapter,
choosing the numbers so that each quantity is exactly reproducible by hand. Recall the setup: the new
inhaled therapy $B$ is compared, unanchored, against comparator $A$ on the binary outcome *severe
exacerbation within 12 months*, analyzed on the log-risk-ratio scale. The IPD outcome model, fitted with a
log link, is
$$
\log P(Y=1\mid x_R,u)=\beta_0+\beta_R\,x_R+\beta_U\,u,
\qquad
\beta_0=-1.0,\ \beta_R=0.4,\ \beta_U=-0.5,
$$
where $x_R$ is the one reported covariate (standardized age) and $u$ the one unreported covariate (baseline
$\mathrm{FEV}_1$, a prognostic factor the comparator did not report). The comparator publication reports the
marginal of $x_R$ as mean
$m_R=1.0$, standard deviation $\sigma_R=0.5$, and its own event risk $\mu_0=0.47$; it does *not* report
$u$. In the IPD, $u$ has mean $\bar{x}_U=2.0$ and standard deviation $\sigma_U=1.0$. For a hand-checkable
marginalization we take $x_R$ and $u$ independent in the comparator population (Gaussian copula equal to
the independence copula) and both normal.

**The sensitivity curve in closed form.** Under independence and normality, the comparator-population risk
of the index treatment is a product of normal moment generating functions. With
$\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=e^{t\mu+t^2\sigma^2/2}$ for $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$,
$$
